def: A network that scores a response with one scalar, trained on preference pairs with the Bradley-Terry loss $-\log\sigma(r_w - r_l)$.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: optimising a policy against a learned reward model while a KL penalty keeps it close to a reference model.
A loss that trains directly on chosen and rejected pairs, $-\log\sigma(\beta[\Delta_w - \Delta_l])$, equivalent to the KL-regularised RLHF objective without a reward model or RL loop.
Training a pretrained model on prompt-response pairs with next-token loss on the response, which teaches it to follow instructions in a chat format.
Excluding prompt tokens from the loss during SFT so that only the response tokens, including the end-of-turn token, produce gradients.
Low-rank adaptation: freeze a weight matrix $W_0$ and learn $\Delta W = \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$, adding only $r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})$ trainable parameters per matrix.
LoRA on top of a frozen base quantised to 4-bit NF4 with double-quantised block scales, about 4.127 bits per weight, so large models fine-tune on small GPUs.
A few training steps run before a real fine-tune to check that loading, generation, training and saving all work, and to measure seconds per step so the full run time can be extrapolated.

Restarting an interrupted training run from its last saved checkpoint, restoring the weights, optimizer and scheduler state instead of starting over. In Hugging Face trainers it is `trainer.train(resume_from_checkpoint=True)`.
Google Colab's paid currency for runtime: each machine type consumes units per hour (a T4 far fewer than an A100), and plans sell a monthly bundle of units.

The number of examples whose gradients are averaged in one optimizer step: per-device micro-batch times gradient-accumulation steps times number of GPUs. It sets the optimisation behaviour, while memory depends only on the micro-batch.

An SFT setting that computes the training loss only on the assistant turns of a conversation, masking system and user tokens. In TRL it requires a chat template with generation markers around assistant output.

Folding a trained LoRA update into the base weights, $W \leftarrow W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$, to produce an ordinary model with no adapter overhead. In PEFT this is `merge_and_unload()`, done on a 16-bit copy of the base.

Loss of previously learned abilities when a model is fine-tuned on a narrow task, for example a SQL adapter that answers general questions with SQL. It is checked by comparing outputs on general probe prompts before and after tuning.

An offline preference method that regresses the log-ratio gap between chosen and rejected answers onto a fixed target 1/(2τ) with a squared loss. Unlike DPO it stops pushing once the target is reached, which resists overfitting deterministic preferences.

A preference method that trains on single answers labelled desirable or undesirable instead of pairs, using a prospect-theory value function measured against a KL reference point. It suits thumbs-up/down feedback and imbalanced labels.
A single-stage method that adds a log-odds-ratio penalty on the rejected answer to an ordinary SFT loss on the chosen answer. It needs no reference model and no separate SFT run.

A reference-free preference method whose reward is the length-normalised (average per-token) log-probability of an answer, compared with a target margin γ. Normalising by length removes the incentive to write longer answers.
A frozen copy of the starting model, usually the SFT model, against which methods such as RLHF, DPO and KTO measure how far the policy has moved. With LoRA it is obtained by disabling the adapters.

Online methods (PPO, RLOO, GRPO) generate fresh answers from the current model during training and learn from their scores; offline methods (DPO, IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO) learn from a fixed dataset collected in advance.

A policy-gradient method that samples a group of completions per prompt and uses each completion's reward relative to the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation, as its advantage. It keeps PPO's clipped objective but needs no value model.

A reward computed by a program that checks the output objectively, such as matching a maths answer or passing unit tests, rather than by a learned reward model. Training on it is called RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR).

A small reward for following a required output layout, such as reasoning followed by an answer in tags. It gives early learning signal but must stay well below the correctness reward or the model learns to be tidy rather than right.
The probability that at least one of k sampled answers to a problem is correct, usually estimated without bias from n samples with c correct as 1 - C(n-c, k)/C(n, k).
An embedding model that encodes queries and documents separately with the same network and compares their vectors by cosine or dot product, so documents can be embedded once and searched quickly.
In contrastive training, using the positives of the other examples in the same batch as wrong answers for each anchor, which gives $B - 1$ negatives per anchor at no labelling cost.

A training passage that looks relevant to a query but does not answer it, usually mined from the base model's top results. It makes the contrastive task harder, but risks being an unlabelled correct answer (a false negative).
An embedding trained so that its first $m$ dimensions, for several nested sizes $m$, each work as a usable smaller embedding, letting you truncate vectors at deployment to save storage.

Normalised discounted cumulative gain at cut-off $k$: a ranking metric that credits each relevant result by $1/\log_2(\text{position} + 1)$ and divides by the score of a perfect ranking, giving a value between 0 and 1.
